title: Teaching about 9/11: History and Memory
author: Lauren Brown
summary: Lauren Brown, a middle school history teacher, argues that the 25th anniversary of September 11 offers a chance to teach students something more valuable than the timeline of that day: the difference between history (making meaning of the past) and memory (evoking feeling in those who lived it). Because today's students and even some teachers have no personal memory of the attacks, Brown structures her lesson around three real curatorial decisions the National September 11 Memorial Museum faced before opening, asking students to debate what should be shown and why before revealing what the museum actually chose. She draws a parallel to the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire to help students reason about similarity and difference across historical tragedies, and closes by pressing on whether empathy belongs inside history instruction or outside it. The piece ultimately argues that a democracy-preparing history curriculum cannot treat empathy as optional, even while acknowledging how politically fraught the framing of any national tragedy has become.
points: Brown structures the lesson around three real museum curatorial dilemmas (e.g., whether to show images of people jumping from the towers) rather than a straight narrative, forcing students to reason about historical judgment before being told what was decided.

She distinguishes history's job (understanding/meaning-making) from a memorial's job (evoking feeling) using a museum director's own words, then uses that tension as the lesson's organizing idea rather than a side note.

The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire is used as a deliberate comparison case, training students to transfer ethical reasoning about spectacle and dignity across two different historical tragedies rather than treating 9/11 as sui generis.

Brown argues empathy in history teaching is not a soft add-on but a civic necessity, tying it directly to the stated purposes of U.S. constitutional democracy rather than leaving it as a matter of teacher temperament.
quotes: Two years before the National September 11 Memorial Museum opened, The New York Times reported on the fraught debates over its creation, when the attacks were still fresh and survivors and their families strongly debated what should and should not be included in its exhibits.

Museums are about understanding, about making meaning of the past, said James Gardner, who oversees the nation's legislative archives, presidential libraries and museums. A memorial fulfills a different need; it's about remembering and evoking feelings in the viewer, and that function is antithetical to what museums do.
But knowing where I was and how I felt is not the same thing as knowing all about what happened on September 11 and why.
I think now of every war memorial I ever yawned through on a class field trip, how someone else's past horror was my vacant diversion and maybe I learned something but I didn't feel anything.

History distances us from the past, in both time and space. That distance can be useful, giving us the perspective to analyze events more clearly. But it can also make it harder to feel the human cost, raising a thorny question: Is it even our job as history teachers to close that gap, to invite students into empathy as well as analysis?

Memorials remind us that history is lived experience, not just a set of facts. Holding space for remembering, for feeling, and for seeing the humanity in others is part of how we nurture the kind of citizens our democracy requires.
